newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Commerzbank seeks fund expertise.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Commerzbank seeks fund expertise.

text.p: By acquiring Montgomery Securities's money management business, Commerzbank AG is not only buying a foothold in U.S. mutual funds but hoping to export expertise to a still-evolving fund industry in Europe.

"They're not just buying a U.S. presence, but a U.S. product that is so evolved, compared to the rest of the world," said Joseph Carrier, U.S. chairman of the investment management group at accounting giant Coopers & Lybrand. "(U.S. funds) are the premiere product in the world for systems, capacity and thought processes."
Montgomery Securities said earlier Tuesday it signed a deal to sell its Montgomery Asset Management unit to Commerzbank. Terms were not disclosed.

Carrier said Commerzbank wants to attach its name to Montgomery niches, and take that to continental Europe. "They're looking for skills to export and take to Europe, where the pension crisis is worse than it is here in U.S.," Carrier said.
Some analysts said that the deal does not fall into the blockbuster category.

"Commerzbank is the third biggest bank in Germany, and Montgomery is interesting, but it's not a leadership firm here," said Michael Lipper, president of Lipper Analytical Services. "They're important, but not market leaders."
Lipper said Montgomery, with its 19 retail no-load funds, is "viewed as a growth operator."
"They're California based, and that translates well overseas," Lipper said. "People tend to think that means technology and growth," which could be a good marketing hook.

Its emerging markets fund, with assets of about $1 billion, outperformed the sector over the last 12 months, with returns of 17.27 percent versus a sector average of 14.10 percent, according to Lipper.
Its $1 billion growth fund lagged the sector, with returns of 13.54 percent versus a group average of 15.35 percent, Lipper said.
Its best performing fund was the smaller equity income, with assets of about $38 million. The fund was up 19.85 percent versus a sector average of 18.19 percent.
Industry analysts said the deal gives Commerzbank more financial products to sell in their own vast bank network.

"I think it would be helpful for them as a route to get the additional distribution in Europe," said one fund industry specialist, who declined to be identified. "Commerzbank is...interested in building asset management."
There have been industry rumors flying for weeks about an impending deal. Carrier speculated that the agreement may have been complicated by worries at Montgomery Asset Management.

"Managers may have been concerned that they built a bit of a franchise, and were anxious to keep together the machine they built," he said. "Price is important, but price isn't the whole deal. They wanted to make sure they had some say in the new company."
Commerzbank is a Coopers & Lybrand client in Germany.
The Montgomery unit has about $8 billion in assets under management in private and institutional accounts and the Montgomery Funds, a family of 19 no-load mutual funds.

The deal continues the trend of European banks buying U.S. asset managers. Dresdner Bank AG bought RCM Capital Management, a San Francisco-based institutional money manager, last year. Industry sources put the purchase price at about $300 million.
Swiss Bank Corp bought Brinson Associates, a Chicago-based institutional money manager, in 1994.
The Montgomery-Commerzbank transaction, subject to approval by the Federal Reserve Board, is expected to close on or about July 31, 1997, Montgomery said.
